text.p: Here are the highlights from Swiss newspapers on Thursday:

- The Swiss government said on Wednesday it wanted a quick resolution of bilateral talks in trade ties European Union, which are stuck over EU demands for lower priced truck access to Swsis tran-Alpine roads. But the cabinet said it would not accept just any settlement. It said the chances of completing the negotiations were still intact.

- The cabinet's 1998 federal budget proposal is nearly finalised. The government unveiled plans to bring down next year's deficit to 5.5 billion francs. The original draft budget had foreseen a deficit of 8.7 billion.

- In a letter to media organisations in Israel, the Swiss embassy in Tel Aviv criticised a BBC-propduced documentary on 'Nazi Gold and Jewish Money'. The film, which was coproduced by Swiss television SF-DRS, has been roundly criticised in Switzerland as an unfair exaggeration of charegs the Swiss profited cynically from World War Two and the Holocaust. Abraham Burg, chairman of the Jewish Agency, and major Israeli newspapers also critizised the film as one-sided.

- A tape of a conversation shows that Swiss right-wing politician Christoph Blocher was wrongly quoted as saying there were no Holocaust victims left. Blocher's statement as quoted by the weekly SonntagsZeitung outraged survivors of the Holocaust. But Swiss television SF-DRS played a tape of the conversation its crew had made, in which Blocher says only that Switzerland cannot pay money to people who have already died.
- Swiss Bank Corp reported a 84 percent boost in net profits to 1,326 million Swiss francs in the 1997 first semester.

- Richard Burt, American adviser for the Swiss government in the United States, said that Switzerland was on the right track to improve its image in the U.S. but needed to do more. - The Swiss Federal Railraods (SBB) reported a 145 million Swiss franc deficit for the first half of 1997. The SBB now expects a full-year deficit of 200 million francs, above a budgeted level of 153 million francs.
